title: STRIDE
summary: STRIDE is a threat enumeration mnemonic that groups threats into six categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. It was developed so that designers without a deep attack background could still systematically ask the right questions about each element of a data-flow diagram. The categories map neatly onto security properties, which is what makes the framework teachable: spoofing attacks authenticity, tampering attacks integrity, repudiation attacks non-repudiation of actions, information disclosure attacks confidentiality, denial of service attacks availability and elevation of privilege attacks authorisation. In practice the mnemonic is applied per element and per flow, with a common convention that processes, data stores, data flows, external entities and trust boundaries each attract a characteristic subset of the six. For a practising engineer STRIDE is most useful as a completeness check rather than a rating scheme, because it deliberately says nothing about likelihood or impact and produces no prioritisation on its own. Teams normally pair it with a scoring method and with attack-library mapping to connect abstract categories to observed adversary behaviour. The known weaknesses are worth stating plainly. STRIDE was framed for classical component-and-network designs and fits cloud identity, serverless and machine-learning pipelines awkwardly. It has no privacy or supply-chain category. Its output is highly dependent on the facilitator's skill, and groups tend to over-report the categories they understand and under-report repudiation and availability. Reviewing a STRIDE session for concrete preconditions and observable failure modes is the cheapest way to raise its quality.
objectives: You will be able to name the six STRIDE categories and state which security property each one attacks.
You will be able to apply the mnemonic element by element to a data-flow diagram without missing entire categories.
You will be able to explain the conventional mapping between diagram element types and the STRIDE categories most likely to apply.
You will be able to convert a bare STRIDE label into a concrete threat statement with preconditions and impact.
You will be able to identify design situations where STRIDE fits poorly, such as cloud identity graphs and machine-learning pipelines.
You will be able to critique a completed STRIDE worksheet for over-reporting and under-reporting bias.

beginner.definition: STRIDE is a checklist of six threat types used when designing a system. The letters stand for spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege. Together they cover faking an identity, changing data, denying an action, leaking secrets, blocking access, and gaining extra rights. Walking the list helps a team spot gaps it might miss.
beginner.whyItMatters: Teams often forget whole kinds of attack because nobody names them out loud. STRIDE gives six simple prompts so no category is quietly skipped. It needs no deep attacker knowledge, which means designers and developers can take part. The result is a list of concrete questions early, when changes are still cheap. Skipping it means discovering the same gaps in production.
howItWorks: Draw your system as boxes for components and arrows for data flows.
Mark the trust boundaries, the lines where data moves between different owners.
For every box and arrow, ask the six STRIDE questions in turn.
Write each threat as a real sentence with an actor, an asset, and an impact.
Rate each threat by how likely it is and how much damage it would cause.
Choose a response for each: fix it, transfer it, accept it, or remove the feature.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel with a checklist for each room: is the lock working, is the window shut, is the safe closed, is the smoke alarm fitted, is the phone working? The cleaner walks the same list in every room. She may find nothing in most, but the one room with a broken lock gets fixed. STRIDE is that room checklist for software design. It makes you look at the same six things everywhere.
takeaways: STRIDE gives six prompts: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, disclosure, denial, and privilege.
Use it as a completeness check, not as a risk score.
Write each threat as a concrete sentence, or no fix will follow.
